## I Introduction

frb are a class of extremely energetic radio transients that are theorized to be associated with neutron stars [105, 86, 88, 19, 115]. To date, thousands of frb have been detected. The majority of these have been discovered using the chime (chime) telescope [16] by the chimefrb (chimefrb) [30]11 1 https://www.chime-frb.ca/voevents. Though the origins of frb remain unknown [66], their dm (dm) as observed by radio telescopes localizes them to extragalactic (and even cosmological) distances [65, 29, 34].

The notable exceptions to this extragalactic consensus are the frb associated with FRB 20200428A. First detected in 2020 April by chimefrb and the stare2 (stare2) [25], FRB 20200428A was quickly found to be associated with the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154, which was undergoing an unusual period of flaring X-ray activity at that time [31, 26, 21, 81]. Simultaneous X-ray observations from Konus-Wind [40], INTEGRAL [78], AGILE [102], and Insight-HXMT [60] led to the first coincident observation of both radio emission and X-rays from an frb source. frb from SGR 1935+2154 were also observed during three other epochs by chimefrb and others, on 2020 October 08, 2022 October 14, and 2022 December 01.22 2 We note that the classification of these radio bursts as frb remains unclear: the SGR 1935+2154 radio bursts are a few orders of magnitude less luminous than typical extragalactic frb, but are still brighter than most giant radio pulses [42]. Bochenek et al. [25] name them as frb while Giri et al. [42] call them frb-like. Here, we describe them as frb. Additionally, X-ray glitches and bursts from SGR 1935+2154 were observed by NICER and NuSTAR during the nine hours surrounding the 2022 October 14 frb [50]. The connection between these X-ray bursts and frb, even from the same magnetar, is not well understood—indeed, radio emission with no coincident X-rays has been detected from SGR 1935+2154 [119] and vice versa [113].

The compact object nature of these powerful transients suggests that gw could also be emitted by the same mechanisms that produce frb. The detection of gw from an frb source (or lack thereof) could help to elucidate the mechanisms behind frb [115], and potentially expand the realm of detected gw beyond those with cbc (cbc) origins.

Previous works by the lvk (lvk) have searched for gw emission coincident with frb [3, 11], as well as for gw from magnetar bursts [5, 6, 72, 12] and pulsar glitches [2, 55, 9] using the Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo gw observatories [1, 14]. While no detections were found in these studies, the searches have established upper limits on gw energy that may have been emitted in association with these events. In particular, Abbott et al. [11] performed a search for gw emission coincident with frb from chimefrb during the O3a LIGO–Virgo observing run, with searches targeted at gw from cbc as well as generic gw transients, setting an upper limit of $10^{51}-10^{57}$ erg of gw energy within 70-3560 Hz. In addition, Abbott et al. [12] placed upper limits on gw energy ( $\sim 10^{43}$ erg) coincident with 11 X-ray and soft gamma-ray magnetar bursts from SGR 1935+2154.

SGR 1935+2154, as the first (and at the time of writing, only) frb source to be confidently associated with a specific neutron-star progenitor, presents a unique opportunity to search for gw when the source is localized to a particular compact object. Additionally, at $\sim 6.6$ kpc [118], it is more than two orders of magnitude nearer to Earth than the next closest frb, which has been localized to the nearby galaxy M81, 3.6 Mpc away [22, 57].

The four periods of frb activity from SGR 1935+2154 fell between the O3 and O4 observing runs of the lvk, when the LIGO and Virgo detectors were offline33 3 https://observing.docs.ligo.org/plan/. Fortunately, GEO600 [47, 68, 15, 38], a gw detector in Hannover, Germany that is operated by members of the LIGO Scientific Collaboration, was observing in Astrowatch mode [46] and collecting gw data during all four periods. The chimefrb events for three of the four periods occurred when GEO600 was in observing mode, while the fourth frb occurred within minutes of when GEO600 was observing (see Sec. III).

In this paper, we analyze GEO600 data to search for gw emission coincident with the four frb observed by chimefrb from SGR 1935+2154. We conduct two searches for unmodeled gw transients: one targeted at short-duration bursts with $\mathcal{O}{\rm(second)}$ durations, and another aimed at long-duration bursts lasting from 1 to 10 seconds. Due to SGR 1935+2154’s proximity, the results constitute the most sensitive searches for gw from frb sources to date, despite GEO600’s lower sensitivity compared to LIGO and Virgo (see Fig. 1). We also search for gw coincident with the two X-ray glitches and the X-ray burst peak observed by NICER and NuSTAR in the hours around the frb on 2022 October 14 [50]. This paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we describe the em (em) observations of frb from SGR 1935+2154. Section III details our short- and long-duration searches for gw, with results presented in Sec. IV. We discuss the implications of these findings and conclude in Sec. V.

While at low frequencies GEO600’s sensitivity is substantially diminished compared to that of the larger detectors, the gap narrows at frequencies around 2 kHz, near the expected neutron-star f-mode frequency.*

## II Fast radio bursts from SGR 1935+2154

The magnetar SGR 1935+2154 was discovered by Swift in 2014 [98, 61]. Since then, it has been highly active, with periods of intense emission in the X-ray and radio [54, 113].

On 2020 April 27, Swift observed multiple X-ray bursts from SGR 1935+2154, suggesting that the magnetar had entered a period of high activity [21]. Less than 24 hours later, chimefrb and stare2 detected an frb from the location of SGR 1935+2154 [31, 26]. Konus-Wind [40], INTEGRAL [78], AGILE [102], and Insight-HXMT [60] observed hard X-rays arriving at the same time, serving as the first ever observation of simultaneous radio and X-ray emission from an frb source. Follow-up radio observations during the same active period by the fast (fast) [116] and radio telescopes from the evn (evn) [56] identified additional radio bursts from SGR 1935+2154, though at lower energies. At higher energies, no gamma-ray emission has been observed from this source [13, 91].

Since 2020 April, SGR 1935+2154 has had multiple periods of high activity leading to the emission of frb. On 2020 October 08, chimefrb observed three frb from SGR 1935+2154 arriving within a few seconds [45, 89, 42]. chimefrb and the gbt (gbt) observed frb again two years later on 2022 October 14, with a chimefrb event surrounded by five gbt frb within 1.5 seconds [37, 70, 42]. During the days around the frb on 2022 October 14, SGR 1935+2154 was undergoing a period of intense X-ray burst activity. This burst storm began on October 10 [77, 80] and was monitored by various telescopes, such as NICER, NuSTAR, and XMM-Newton (see, e.g., Hu et al. 50, Ibrahim et al. 52), which detected hundreds of milliseconds- to seconds-long bursts of high-energy photons. The X-ray burst rate peaked during a flare 2.5 hr ( $\pm$ 1 min) before the frb and then steadily decreased over the next hours [50]. In addition, the high-cadence monitoring observations allowed accurate measurements of the spin rate of SGR 1935+2154 (nominally 0.308 Hz; Israel et al. 54). The evolution of the spin rate showed that SGR 1935+2154 underwent a spin-up glitch about 4.4 hr ( $\pm$ 30 min) before the frb and another spin-up glitch about 4.4 hr ( $\pm$ 30 min) after the frb, while the magnetar’s spin-down rate between these two glitches was about one hundred times higher than its normal rate [50]. X-ray bursts were also detected by GECAM and HEBS [107] and Konus-Wind [40] arriving within the expected frb dispersion time. In addition to the NICER and NuSTAR observations mentioned above [39], Insight-HXMT [60] also observed X-rays from SGR 1935+2154 during this active period, though at the time of the frb all three were occulted by the Earth. Finally, a fourth frb was detected by chimefrb on 2022 December 01 [85, 42], accompanied by a faint hard X-ray signal detected by Fermi-GBM [112].

Most estimates and methods place the distance to SGR 1935+2154 between 1.5 and 15 kpc [83, 84, 99, 58, 95, 117, 118, 20]. We adopt the determination by Zhou et al. [118] of 6.6 $\pm$ 0.7 kpc, falling near the mean of the measurements.

Despite this reduced brightness compared to the typical frb population, SGR 1935+2154’s proximity as the only known Galactic frb source means that it presents the most promising opportunity to date for multiwavelength and multimessenger studies of frb emitters.

### II.1 Models for coincident GW-FRB emission

Magnetars have long been theorized to be progenitors of frb [88]. The detection of frb from SGR 1935+2154, a well-studied magnetar, has now confirmed this association for at least some frb, though the exact emission mechanism remains unclear [69, 115].

Most models which predict gw emission from frb progenitors assume a cbc association, such as during or after the final stages of the cbc inspiral [108, 111], long before the cbc merger through interactions of magnetospheres [114], or other interactions of compact binaries with their environments (see Platts et al. [88] for a review of frb theory). Prior studies such as Abbott et al. [11] have searched for gw from these sources using targeted matched-filter analyses, aimed at cbc sources. Since SGR 1935+2154 is not in a compact binary [33] and has exhibited multiple periods of frb activity, we do not expect cbc-like gw emission from this source. Instead, as a magnetar, we can focus on only a few possible emission mechanisms for gw coincident with frb. In particular, because gw are induced by time-varying quadrupole moments, we review models which predict em magnetar activity associated with such moments.

Since at least some frb originate from magnetars, theories have drawn connections between them and magnetar giant flares [103, 74, 28], which are are thought to be powered by magnetic activity near the surface of a neutron star [104, 41]. These giant flares are rare but so energetic that gw emission may be detectable due to hydromagnetic coupling of the magnetic dipole to the mass quadrupole [53, 35]. Quasi-periodic oscillations in the X-ray tails of giant flares may also create gw through torsional or Alfvén modes which alter the star’s quadrupole moment [59, 44, 93]. While no giant flares from SGR 1935+2154 were detected during its periods of frb activity, the coincident X-ray activity suggests a potential link in the provenance of the high-energy em emission.

Crustal f-modes are a possible source of transient gw from isolated neutron stars [43, 49]. These typically fall at around 2 kHz [18], near the frequencies where GEO600 is most sensitive (see Fig. 1).

Moreover, neutron-star glitches, such as those from SGR 1935+2154 in 2022 October investigated in this work, may emit gw potentially observable by current gw detectors [92, 109, 76]. Previous limits were derived for the Vela pulsar (located at 290 pc; Dodson et al. [36]) glitch in 2006, providing limits on the emitted gw energy of the order of 1045 erg [2].

## III Search for gravitational waves

Using data from GEO600, we search for generic gw transients from SGR 1935+2154 around the times of four frb detected by chimefrb. GEO600 is a dual-recycled Michelson interferometer with folded arms and takes astrophysical observations in the 40 Hz - 6 kHz frequency band when operating in Astrowatch mode [46]. Over the past two decades, it has pioneered several key technologies for gw detectors [15, 67]. GEO600 has lower sensitivity compared to the Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo detectors ( $\sim 10^{-22}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ at 1 kHz, see Fig. 1), but has strengths in uptime. It continued taking observations during the initial period of the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent LIGO and Virgo upgrades throughout 2020-2022, during which chimefrb observed these frb from SGR 1935+2154.

Given the unknown nature of the emission mechanism of the frb, we search for generic transient gravitational-wave signals present in the GEO600 data using two unmodeled burst searches: PySTAMP [73], targeted at long-duration bursts with lengths from 1 to 10 s, and X-Pipeline [101, 110], for short-duration bursts lasting less than 1 s. Previous searches for gw coincident with frb, such as the ones presented in Abbott et al. [11], also considered a possible cbc origin for the gw emission; the non-compact binary nature of SGR 1935+2154 precludes the use of cbc matched-filter searches. Given that SGR 1935+2154 is a magnetar, we follow the previous gw magnetar study presented in Abbott et al. [12] and employ PySTAMP to perform a long-duration search, which has not previously been used for gw frb analyses. Additionally, prior searches have typically been restricted to coincidences with frb where data from at least two gw detectors is available. For these frb from SGR 1935+2154, only GEO600 was observing, so we employ a single-detector search. This limits our ability to veto candidates based on coherence between detectors and the amount of background that can be estimated, reducing the search sensitivity, but given the extraordinary nature of these frb, we determined that a single-detector search in GEO600 data was warranted.

This allows us to probe a broad parameter space while keeping the detector behavior relatively stationary. We also employ a compact $[-4,4]$ s search window in the short-duration search to probe the time immediately surrounding the frb with higher sensitivity. In addition, we search for emission around the time of three X-ray events detected by NuSTAR and NICER on 2022 October 14. These events consisted of a spin-up glitch, a peak in the X-ray burst emission, and another spin-up glitch. Since the uncertainty in their times is greater than a minute, we only perform an extended-window search, targeting a symmetric $[-1000,1000]$ s window, subject to data availability. We restrict our search to frequencies from 300 Hz to 4096 Hz, with the lower cutoff set by the low frequency sensitivity of GEO600 and the upper cutoff aiming to capture neutron-star crustal f-modes, which are predicted to fall at approximately 2 kHz [18].

### III.1 Simulated waveforms to quantify sensitivity

We measure the sensitivity of our search by inserting simulated waveforms (“injections”) into the off-source data and quantifying the pipeline’s ability to recover them. For the short-duration X-Pipeline search, these injections are largely the same as those used in Abbott et al. [11]. The waveforms include Sine-Gaussians and damped sinusoids and are summarized in Table 2. We briefly describe each waveform family below:

- • Sine-Gaussians: The majority of the simulated waveforms we use are Sine-Gaussians, which can model starquakes and certain neutron-star f-modes. They are described in Eq. 1 of Abbott et al. [4]. Most of these injections are performed with inclinations chosen randomly, but we also employ some optimally inclined (circular polarization only, emitted face-on to the observer) waveforms near the expected f-modes at $\sim$ 2000 Hz to better constrain our sensitivity to these models. In all the injected waveforms, we use a quality factor $Q=9$ (the approximate number of cycles in the waveform) following Abbott et al. [8], Abbott et al. [11], with central frequencies $f_{0}$ spanning from 300 Hz to 3560 Hz, as shown in Table 2.

- • Damped sinusoids: We also use damped sinusoids to characterize any ringdown behavior in the magnetar. The waveform is described in Eq. C12 of Abbott et al. [12]. These are placed at two frequencies, 1590 Hz and 2020 Hz, to represent plausible f-mode signals. For each frequency, we use two damping timescales to probe a larger parameter space.

The waveforms used by the long-duration PySTAMP analysis are also Sine-Gaussians, but with a duration parameter of 10 s. They are also described in Table 2.

### III.2 Long-duration search with PySTAMP

We use PySTAMP [73] to target gw signals with durations longer than $1$ s around the three frb with coincident GEO600 data. The background distribution and the detection efficiency of the search are characterized using an off-source window that consists of $\sim 12$ hr of data centered on the event time, excluding the on-source window described above. The workflow of the pipeline is as follows. The data are first down-sampled from $16384$ Hz to $8192$ Hz, and then high-pass filtered with a frequency cutoff of $40$ Hz to remove potential spectral leakage from lower frequencies. After these preprocessing steps, the resulting time series are split into $1$ s Hann-windowed segments with $50\%$ overlap. The fast Fourier transform is computed over each segment to build a time-frequency map (tf-map) with a resolution of $1$ s $\times 1$ Hz. For each frequency bin, the psd (psd) is estimated by taking the median of the squared modulus of the Fourier transform over $1320$ s of adjacent data (similar to Welch’s method but using the median instead of the mean), and a snr (snr) tf-map is built by dividing the value of the Fourier transform in each pixel by the square root of the psd. To identify candidate gw events, a pattern recognition algorithm is run over the tf-map. We use the burstegard algorithm [90] which identifies clusters of neighboring pixels whose snr is above a threshold of $2.5$ . Clusters consisting of $5$ or more pixels are saved as candidate gw events. Each cluster is then assessed a ranking statistic $\Lambda$ that is the sum of the snr of each of its pixels divided by the square root of the total number of pixels.

Clusters found in the off-source window form the background of the search and are used to estimate the far (far) of clusters found in the on-source window as a function of the ranking statistic $\Lambda$ . PySTAMP is primarily intended to work on cross-correlated data from a pair of independent detectors, which allows for the simulation of an extended amount of background by shifting the time series of one detector with respect to the other. Such a method cannot be applied here in the single-detector GEO600 search. Hence, the background lifetime is limited to the duration of the off-source window, so the far of each cluster can only be estimated down to a minimum of $\sim 1$ per $12$ hours ( $2.3\times 10^{-5}$ Hz). See Sec. V for further discussion of the limited far.

Noise from gw detectors typically features narrowband spectral artifacts that appear as horizontal lines in a time-frequency representation (or vertical lines in the amplitude spectral density; see Fig. 1). Because the psd is estimated for each frequency bin by taking the median over neighboring time segments, most of these lines are correctly factored into the psd and do not generate high snr pixels. However, we observe an excess of clusters in the off-source window around some specific frequencies, likely due to fluctuations of spectral lines around their central values. We therefore remove clusters for a narrow range of frequencies corresponding to known GEO600 spectral lines. In order to reject short, broadband noise transients (known as glitches), we also remove clusters for which more than $30\%$ of the total energy is contained within a single $1$ s time segment.

### III.3 Short-duration search with X-Pipeline

We perform a search for short-duration unmodeled gw transients using X-Pipeline [101, 110]. While typically run as a coherent search across multiple detectors (such as in previous searches for gw from frb [11], grb [8, 10], and magnetars [12]), we use X-Pipeline in a single-detector mode because GEO600 was the only gw detector collecting data at the time of the frb. X-Pipeline splits the psd-whitened data into 64 s segments, then applies a Fourier transform to produce time-frequency maps. The time-frequency pixels with amplitudes in the highest 1% that neighbor each other are clustered into candidate detection events. Each event is then assigned a ranking statistic based on the summed energy contained in the pixels. To determine the significance of these candidate events, we compare them against a distribution of background energies empirically measured in an identical manner from an “off-source” period. This is chosen to fall around (but not including) the time of the on-source data and to be long enough to allow for meaningful significances to be calculated but not so long that the detector’s behavior is nonstationary. We employ a 24-hour off-source window, symmetric about each event’s time.

When X-Pipeline is run on data from multiple detectors as is typical, vetoes of problematic event candidates can be applied by utilizing the presumed coherence of any real gw event across detectors. This is unfortunately not an option in a single-detector search such as this, meaning that the search becomes more vulnerable to background noise. To improve the sensitivity of our search, we apply frequency-domain vetoes based on the distribution of time-frequency candidate events in the off-source window for each frb search. We veto narrow frequency bands ( $\sim 10$ Hz bandwidth) where there is considerable excess noise; most of these vetoes corresponded to known spectral lines from the GEO600 detector.

We do not find any candidate gw events in either the long-duration or short-duration compact-window searches for any of the frb. For the long-duration PySTAMP search, no triggers survive the cuts described in Sec. III.2 for the 2020 April and 2022 October frb. Five triggers survive for the 2020 October frb, but the loudest trigger has a far of $\sim 1$ per 1000 s with a p-value of 0.76 and is thus not significant. In the short-duration X-Pipeline case, only the 2020 April, 2020 October, and 2022 October frb compact-window searches had enough background to be considered useful for gw searches, as described above. The only surviving trigger from these three searches is from the 2022 October frb and has a p-value of 0.53, and thus is also not significant.

For the short-duration extended-window searches, long off-source windows are required to estimate the background, and the single-detector nature of this search prevents the use of “time-slides” between multiple detectors to artificially generate background. These limitations mean that for the extended-window short-duration searches, there are sometimes as few as six off-source background trials, limiting any potential detection’s maximum significance to a p-value of $1/6\approx 0.17$ —insufficient for any meaningful statement about the astrophysical nature of any outlier in the data. Thus, instead of reporting potential gw candidates from the extended-window searches with inconsequential statements about significance, we decided to use the searches only to determine the loudest trigger within the on-source window for a given waveform model, thereby setting an upper limit on the corresponding gw energy. This is the “loudest event statistic” [23, 24].

For all searches and windows (listed in Table 1), we estimate the root-sum-square signal amplitude of the gw strain $h_{\rm rss}$ (see Eqs. 3 and 4 of Sutton [100]) at 50% and 90% detection efficiency to set upper limits on the gw energy emitted. To convert the $h_{\rm rss}$ values for each injection type that are output by the search pipelines to energy, we use (following Sutton [100])

$$ E_{\rm GW}=\frac{2}{5}\frac{\pi^{2}c^{3}}{G}D_{L}^{2}f_{0}^{2}h_{\rm rss}^{2}, $$

with $f_{0}$ describing the central frequency of each injection and $D_{L}$ set to the 6.6 kpc distance of SGR 1935+2154 [118]. The results of the long-duration search are shown in Tab. 3. The 50% and 90% limits from the short-duration analysis are shown in Tab. 4 and Tab. 5 respectively. We show in Fig. 3 our 90% upper limits from both the long- and short-duration analyses as a function of frequency, corresponding to the upper limits at which 90% of the injected signals were recovered. To be explicit, the $X$ % $h_{\rm rss}$ value for a given waveform model (and corresponding gw energy) is calculated by finding the $h_{\rm rss}$ at which $X$ % of the injected waveforms are recovered (i.e., found with a significance higher than the loudest non-injection event in the window).

For some injections in the short-duration search (mostly those at lower frequencies such as SG-D with $f_{0}=300$ Hz), limits could not be established because noise in the detector prevented sufficient recovery of the injected signals. Limited data availability and poor data quality around the time of the 2020 October 08 event meant that no injection reached 90% recovery, leading to the lack of 90% limits.

The nondetection of gw emission from our analyzed frb implies that the gw-to-radio energy ratio must be less than $E_{\rm GW}/E_{\rm radio}\sim 8\times 10^{14}$ at the 90% level, for a time window from [-4, 4] s at a gw frequency of approximately 300 Hz. At the $\sim 2$ kHz frequencies close to the neutron-star f-mode, $E_{\rm GW}/E_{\rm radio}\lesssim 1.7\times 10^{16}$ at the 90% level. The gw and radio energies for our analyzed frb are shown in Fig. 4, alongside the same quantities for frb from O3a analyzed in Abbott et al. [11].

## V Discussion and conclusion

The previous best limits on coincident gw emission with frb were set by Abbott et al. [11] using extragalactic frb observed during the O3a lvk observing run, using SG waveforms and X-Pipeline. Fig. 3 shows the 90% upper limits on the gw energy during our analyzed frb from SGR 1935+2154, compared previous limits presented as a range spanning the best and worst 90% limits from Abbott et al. [11]. In the short-duration search at approximately 300 Hz, the best previous 90% upper limit on gw energy was set at $3.4\times 10^{51}$ erg; at approximately 2 kHz, the best previous 90% upper limit was $7.9\times 10^{54}$ erg. We improve on the 300 Hz constraint by about two orders of magnitude, and the 2 kHz constraint by over four orders of magnitude. No previous long-duration searches around frb events have been performed, so the long-duration search results presented here represent the first constraints on such emission. Studies have predicted that magnetar flares can emit up to $10^{48}-10^{49}$ erg in gw energy near the f-mode for $\sim 200$ ms [53, 35]—a regime that is probed by our most stringent 50% short-duration constraints at approximately 2 kHz (see SG-H waveform in Table 4). We also slightly improve the upper limit on $E_{\rm GW}/E_{\rm radio}$ , as shown in Fig. 4.

We note that our results are not the most constraining limits on gw emission from the magnetar SGR 1935+2154, which are reported in Abbott et al. [12] in a search for gw emission around times of magnetar X-ray and gamma-ray flares. The relationship between these magnetar bursts and frb is poorly understood, but are likely to be caused by different physical processes, even if the underlying magnetar behavior may be related [106]. Hence, both gw limits are complementary and can help to better understand the emission mechanisms at play. Considering the X-ray spin-up glitches, our best limits on the emitted gw energy ( $\sim 10^{51}$ erg at 300 Hz) are still far from the X-ray measured changes in rotational energy ( $\sim 10^{42}$ erg from Hu et al. [50]).

Since $E_{\rm GW}\propto D_{L}^{2}$ in Eq. 1, our constraints are heavily dependent on the distance to SGR 1935+2154. As mentioned in Sec. II, estimates for SGR 1935+2154’s distance vary by almost an order of magnitude. If its true distance is as close as the 1.5 kpc measured by Bailes et al. [20], our energy constraints would improve by a factor of almost 20. On the other hand, if SGR 1935+2154 is at almost 15 kpc, as suggested by Surnis et al. [99], our constraints would worsen by a factor of 5.

As a single-detector search, the number of possible background trials (and thus the assessment of gw candidates via p-value or far) is limited by the time in which the detector behavior remains similar to that of the on-source window. For example, the minimum far for the long-duration PySTAMP search was limited to $\sim$ 1 per 12 hours. Since we do not recover any candidates in the on-source windows which appear to differentiate themselves from the background, we did not have to assess any candidate’s significance beyond 1 per 12 hours, meaning that this limitation did not affect our results. However, future single-detector searches may encounter the problem where a candidate in the on-source window is unlike anything found in the background trials, complicating an accurate assessment of its significance. Some gw cbc searches have implemented techniques to improve single-detector significance estimation [97, 27]; unmodeled searches like PySTAMP and X-Pipeline may also benefit from such enhancements.

At the time of writing, no frb have been detected from SGR 1935+2154 since 2022. The O4 observing run of the lvk, with participation from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detectors will continue until mid-2025. Given the increased sensitivity of these detectors compared to GEO600, any SGR 1935+2154 frb during the remainder of O4 could provide another opportunity to probe the gw–frb connection.

# Neutron Star–Primordial Black Hole Binaries: Dynamical Tides, Resonance Locking, and Gravitational Waves

**Authors:** Isaac Legred Email: ilegred2@illinois.edu Affiliation: Illinois Center for Advanced Studies of the Universe, Department of Physics, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, Illinois, 61801, USA Nicolás Yunes Affiliation: Illinois Center for Advanced Studies of the Universe, Department of Physics, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, Illinois, 61801, USA

## Abstract

The orbital evolution of a neutron star and a much lower-mass primordial black hole can differ strikingly from that of typical compact binaries. Dynamical tides, analogous to those in the Solar System’s giant planet-moon systems, can accelerate inspiral or induce outspiral, depending on the orbital configuration. We show how gravitational-wave emission mediates this evolution when neutron star modes remain locked in resonance with the orbit. These effects may leave observable signatures in pulsar timing or gravitational waves.

Introduction. Compact binary inspirals are generally studied using the well-understood model of two structureless point masses in general relativity [1]. Effects that go beyond this point-particle model, such as matter effects in neutron stars, are treated as small perturbations [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. The motivation for this perturbative treatment is the exceptionally strong scaling of equilibrium tidal effects with orbital separation ( $r^{-5}$ ). Beyond a certain orbital separation, tidal effects are assumed to be completely negligible in compact binary inspirals. However, the weakness of tidal effects is not a property of relativity, but rather simply Newtonian gravity [9, 10] applied to compact stars.

The difficulty of explaining the rapid orbital migration of Jupiter and Saturn’s moons with equilibrium tides [11, 12] motivated Fuller et al. [13] to consider dynamical tides. Dynamical tides arise when a companion’s time-dependent tidal field excites internal waves or oscillation modes in an extended body. When the tidal forcing frequency approaches a mode frequency, resonant coupling can enhance the exchange of energy and angular momentum between the body and the orbit, producing a large response even if the tidal field is weak. In giant planet–moon systems, this enhanced coupling can transfer angular momentum from the planet’s rotation to the moon’s orbit and drive rapid outward migration.

The obvious limitation of explaining secular orbital changes using dynamical tides is that the large effects of resonant energy transfer are only active so long as the mode remains resonantly coupled to the orbit. If the orbit changes, and the internal mode frequency does not, then the resonance is lost. However, in certain cases, stable equilibrium configurations in the phase space of orbital parameters and internal dynamical degrees of freedom appear, which prevent large departures of the orbital frequency from the mode frequency. This process is termed resonance locking [14].

Once resonance locking occurs, the mode and the orbit evolve together as the mode frequency changes. In the case of Jupiter’s and Saturn’s moons, this evolution is driven by changes in the giants’ internal structure. In the case of comparable-mass neutron-star binaries, earlier calculations that neglected nonlinear hydrodynamics found that gravitational-wave inspiral is too rapid for tidal spin evolution to maintain resonance [15, 16]. More recently, however, calculations including nonlinear hydrodynamics have found that the resulting amplitude-dependent shifts of low-order neutron-star g-mode frequencies may allow a mode to remain near resonance with the tidal forcing as the inspiral proceeds [17, 18]. Nonetheless, it remains unclear to what extent double neutron star binaries can have their evolution substantially modified by resonance-locked energy transfer.

How does resonance locking then affect compact binary inspiral? Resonance locking in inspiraling double white dwarf binaries was studied by Refs. [19, 16]. Because the stellar moments of inertia are small compared with the orbital moment of inertia, the orbital dynamics are only weakly modified by resonance locking, while the spins evolve on the gravitational-wave timescale. While neutron stars have very different internal physics than giant planets (or even white dwarfs), their coupled spin and orbital evolution during an established resonance lock is constrained by angular-momentum (and energy) balance. The internal physics determines only whether that lock can be established and maintained.

For resonance locking to occur, tidal oscillation modes must have time to build sufficient amplitude near resonance. In relativistic binaries, this requires the gravitational-wave driven inspiral to be sufficiently slow. For comparable-mass binaries (such as double white dwarfs), the inspiral is slower at large orbital separations, where the orbital dynamics are approximately Newtonian. For extreme mass-ratio binaries, inspiral is also slow even at smaller separations because gravitational waves remove only a small fraction of the orbital angular momentum per dynamical time.

In this Letter, we investigate the orbital dynamics of a neutron star in a binary with a much lower mass compact companion. We find that such a binary can lead to diverse and strikingly different binary behavior than for comparable-mass binaries on the gravitational-wave inspiral timescale. We first consider the necessary conditions in a neutron-star/compact companion binary to establish resonance locking. We then move onto the dynamics of a system that maintains resonance locking, and compute the modifications to the first post-Newtonian equations of motion. We continue by considering the long-term observable implications of resonance locking, and identify a special orbital binary configuration where resonance locking must break down. We finally comment on the astrophysical implications of resonance locking becoming active for the possible case of low-mass primordial black hole that inspirals into a neutron star. If primordial black holes with masses smaller than $\sim 10^{-4}\,M_{\odot}$ exist and form tight binaries with neutron stars, resonance locking may provide a channel to delay or avoid merger that destroys the star.

Resonance locking of neutron-star g-modes. Neutron stars with chemical stratification display a forest of g-modes with frequencies $\lesssim 200\ \mathrm{Hz}$ [20, 21]. The highest of these frequencies is ultimately set by the geometry of the star and the Brunt-Väisälä frequency, i.e. the buoyancy frequency at which a slightly displaced fluid element oscillates about its original position in a stably stratified fluid. At some lower frequency, the g-mode forest terminates because the mode periods are longer than the relevant weak reaction rates in the star [20, 22], though at which frequency this happens is highly uncertain due to poorly constrained microphysics. For cold nucleonic stars, this frequency is likely no more than $1\,\rm{Hz}$ [20, 23], which is the characteristic value we use here.

The tidal force of a companion object on a neutron star drives oscillation modes in the latter. If we define

$$ \sigma=m(\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}-\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}})\,, $$

where $\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is the orbital frequency, then the resonance condition is [23, 24]

$$ \omega_{X}=\left|\sigma\right|, $$

for a mode of frequency $\omega_{X}$ . For example, an $\ell=m=2$ g-mode of frequency $\Omega_{g,\ell=m=2}/2\pi\sim 10\ \rm{Hz}$ of a neutron star with spin frequency $\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}/2\pi\sim 10\ \mathrm{Hz}$ would lock to a companion in a $\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}/2\pi\sim 5\ \mathrm{Hz}$ orbit. However, the opposite ordering of $\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is possible, in which case angular momentum flows from the orbit to the neutron star.

Generally, tidal modifications to the spin depend sensitively on the rate of dissipation in the deformed body, which for neutron stars is assumed to be small. For example, Bildsten and Cutler [25] showed that the collective tidal angular momentum transfer during a typical double neutron star inspiral is insufficient to tidally lock the binary components to one another. They, however, assumed an equilibrium tidal model, which, as we have already discussed, is unable to substantially alter the behavior of the binary. We must then consider the dynamics of tides to assess whether their conclusion remains robust in tight compact binaries.

For dynamical tides, the tidal torque is typically proportional to the quality factor of the mode, rather than inversely proportional to it [9, 23, 19], at least if the inspiral is sufficiently slow to (approximately) saturate the resonance. For neutron star g-modes that may have quality factors of order $\gtrsim 10^{8}$ [20], the tidal torque could be large and locking is promising. The main impediment to locking is very low overlaps between neutron star g-modes and the tidal field of the companion. We estimate in the Supplemental Material that neutron star g-modes down to $\sim 10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ may be able to lock solely through linear response. At lower frequencies, locking may still be possible, but it will likely require nonlinear interactions between shorter-wavelength (higher-order) modes [26, 27]. Such interactions depend on poorly constrained dense-matter physics. Once a resonance lock is established, however, the resonance condition and angular-momentum balance constrain the coupled spin and orbital evolution. We therefore determine the conditions under which a sustained lock accelerates inspiral or induces outspiral, and assess the observational implications.

We begin by deriving the equations of motion for a binary system with an extended compact body and a much smaller compact body in a leading (nontrivial) order post-Newtonian orbit and in full generality. We consider the more massive, geometrically larger object to be a neutron star with mass $M_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , and the smaller body to be a small (sub-solar mass) black hole with mass $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$ , though this fact is not important for this derivation. The equations of motion for the angular momenta are

$$ \displaystyle\dot{L}_{\mathrm{orb}} \displaystyle=\tau_{\mathrm{tide}}+\tau_{\rm GW};\qquad\dot{L}_{\mathrm{NS}}=-\tau_{\mathrm{tide}}, $$

where $\tau_{\rm GW}$ is the leading-order post-Newtonian gravitational-wave torque, and $\tau_{\mathrm{tide}}$ (which we calculate under various hypotheses below) is the torque of the body on the orbit. To enforce the resonance locking condition, we convert the angular momenta into angular velocities

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}} \displaystyle=L_{\mathrm{orb}}/I_{\mathrm{orb}};\qquad\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}=L_{\mathrm{NS}}/I_{\mathrm{NS}}, $$

where $I_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is the effective orbital moment of inertia, given, again at leading order and for a quasi-circular orbit, by

$$ I_{\mathrm{orb}}=M_{\mathrm{BH}}r^{2}=M_{\mathrm{BH}}(GM_{\mathrm{NS}})^{2/3}\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}^{-4/3}, $$

where $r$ is the orbital separation and we have used Kepler’s third law. Equation (3) then becomes

$$ \displaystyle\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}} \displaystyle=\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{tide}}+\tau_{\mathrm{GW}}}{I_{\rm orb}}-\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}\frac{\dot{I}_{\mathrm{orb}}}{I_{\mathrm{orb}}};\qquad\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{NS}}=\frac{-\tau_{\mathrm{tide}}}{I_{\mathrm{NS}}}, $$

because the neutron star moment of inertia $I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ is constant. Differentiating Eq. (5) and simplifying, these become (c.f. Eq. (7) of Ref. [19])

$$ \displaystyle\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}} \displaystyle=-3\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{tide}}+\tau_{\mathrm{GW}}}{I_{\mathrm{orb}}};\qquad\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{NS}}=\frac{-\tau_{\rm tide}}{I_{\mathrm{NS}}}. $$

Interestingly, because of the dependence of the effective orbital moment of inertia on the total angular momentum of the orbit, both $\Omega$ ’s exhibit the same-sign response to tidal angular momentum transfer. That is, when one increases, so will the other, and vice-versa. In order to maintain the resonance locking criterion, $\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{NS}}=\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}}$ , a particular value of $\tau_{\mathrm{tide}}$ must be chosen:

$$ \tau_{\mathrm{tide}}=\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{GW}}}{\left(I_{\mathrm{orb}}/(3I_{\rm NS})-1\right)}. $$

Equation (8) implies that without gravitational-wave torque, given our hypotheses (in particular that the neutron star moment of inertia $I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ and mode frequencies $\omega_{X}$ do not evolve), no tidal torquing can occur. Therefore, the inclusion of relativity induces an additional channel for resonance locking not present in the purely Newtonian case. Physically speaking, this is because gravitational waves serve as a sink for angular momentum; the process would otherwise be kinematically forbidden. Additionally, as is standard, the tide must be passive, so the average rate of energy dissipation inside the neutron star, $\dot{Q}$ must be positive. Assuming an insignificant amount of energy is stored in the mode itself, this fixes the sign of $\sigma$ to be the same as $\tau_{\rm tide}$ , as

$$ \dot{Q}=\frac{\sigma}{m}\tau_{\mathrm{tide}}. $$

Orbital and spin dynamics during resonance lock. Resonance locking of neutron star g-modes to a small compact object can occur in two different regimes, based on where the resonance lock initiates. To understand these two regimes, let us substitute Eq. (8) into Eq. (7) to find

$$ \frac{\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}}}{\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}}^{\rm GW}}=\frac{I_{\mathrm{orb}}}{I_{\mathrm{orb}}-3I_{\mathrm{NS}}}, $$

where $\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}}^{\rm GW}=-3\tau_{\mathrm{GW}}/I_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is the frequency evolution due to gravitational-wave emission alone, evaluated at the same orbital separation. Therefore, the two regimes depend on whether locking is established when $I_{\mathrm{orb}}>3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ or when $I_{\mathrm{orb}}<3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ .

If the resonance lock is initiated with $I_{\mathrm{orb}}>3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , then ${\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}}}/{\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}}^{\rm GW}}>1$ , and the inspiral is accelerated. Physically, the tidal torque transfers angular momentum from the orbit to the neutron star, so this configuration requires $\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}-\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}>0$ . As a result, the neutron star spins up because its spin angular momentum increases, and the small black-hole companion inspirals faster, because the orbital angular momentum decreases faster than it would under gravitational-wave emission alone. As the body inspirals, the effective orbital moment of inertia decreases with the orbital separation, while the neutron star moment of inertia remains constant. As $I_{\mathrm{orb}}$ approaches $3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ from above, the tidal torque required to maintain the resonance lock grows without bound in this description. Before this though, the description of the system we provide breaks down.

If the resonance lock is initiated with $I_{\mathrm{orb}}<3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , then $\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}}<0$ , and the companion begins to outspiral. Physically, the tidal torque feeds angular momentum from the faster-spinning neutron star to the orbit at a rate greater than that removed by gravitational-wave emission. This configuration requires $\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}>\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}$ . As the companion outspirals, the effective orbital moment of inertia increases with the orbital separation, while the neutron star moment of inertia remains constant. As $I_{\mathrm{orb}}$ approaches $3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ from below, the tidal torque required to maintain the resonance lock again grows without bound, though the model surely breaks down before this occurs.

Figure 1 illustrates the two regimes of resonance-locked orbital evolution. In the left panel, locking begins when $I_{\mathrm{orb}}>3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , and the orbital frequency increases more rapidly than predicted from gravitational-wave emission alone, accelerating the inspiral. In the right panel, locking begins when $I_{\mathrm{orb}}<3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , and the orbital frequency decreases despite continued gravitational-wave emission, so the binary outspirals. In the second case, the spin of the NS serves as the reservoir of energy for the system, so the total gravitational-wave energy emitted over the $\sim\mathrm{years}$ -long inspiral-outspiral is much larger than the initial orbital energy of the primordial black hole.

Astrophysical implications. Our calculations apply to any binary composed of a geometrically large, gravitationally compact object and a much lower mass companion, but the prototypical case is a neutron star with a subsolar-mass primordial black hole. The abundance of subsolar mass black holes is constrained by dark matter searches, which imply that black holes in the mass range $\sim(10^{-6}$ – $10^{-2})\,M_{\odot}$ can represent no more than $\lesssim 1\%$ of dark matter [28, 29, 30, 31]. Assuming a typical dark matter density of $\sim 0.5\,\rm{GeV/cm^{3}}$ ( $\approx 0.013\,M_{\odot}/\rm{pc}^{3}$ ) and a primordial black hole fraction of $1\%$ , this leaves $\lesssim 130$ such black holes per cubic parsec. At lower masses, a larger fraction of dark matter may be black holes, and a larger number of black holes are present per unit mass; therefore, the number density of lower-mass primordial black holes is possibly much larger. Per the arguments above, lower mass black holes are likely to outspiral if resonance locked to neutron star g-modes. Therefore close capture scenarios may not necessarily lead to neutron star destruction [32, 33] if resonance locking is generic for these systems, as we discuss further in the End Matter.

Another astrophysical implication of resonance locking applies to pulsar binaries. Observationally, if the neutron star in question is a pulsar, the presence of a $10^{-3}\,M_{\odot}$ companion should be quite evident, unless the orbit is very tight. Low-mass companions with masses $\sim 10^{-8}$ – $10^{-3}\,M_{\odot}$ have been detected around pulsars [34, 35, 36], demonstrating that neutron stars can host companions with very small mass ratios. Dynamical exchange has been proposed to explain the planetary companion orbiting the neutron star–white dwarf binary PSR B1620-26 [37]. While most pulsar planets have long orbital periods ( $\gtrsim 1\,{\rm day}$ ), at least one has been observed with a mass $\sim 10^{-3}\,M_{\odot}$ and a period of $\sim 2.2\,{\rm h}$ [38]. Detecting a planetary-mass companion to a pulsar with an orbital period $\lesssim 1\,{\rm s}$ would demonstrate the existence of an exceptionally dense low-mass object, since an ordinary planet would be tidally disrupted in such an orbit. However, the impact of such a planet on the pulse profile of a $\sim\mathrm{Hz}$ spin-frequency pulsar may be complicated.

Substantially lower-mass objects, $\lesssim 10^{-10}\,M_{\odot}$ , and objects in very tight orbits, may lie unresolved by pulsar timing [39]. The NANOGrav 15-year dataset contains 68 well-timed millisecond pulsars, with timing precision of $\sim 1\,\mu\rm{s}$ [40]. Thus, while detectability depends on the pulsar’s timing noise, the orbital inclination, and the observing baseline, pulsars in binaries with center-of-mass-to-barycenter distances of about $0.1\,$ km (provided their period is $\lesssim 1\,\textrm{yr}$ ) should have visible modifications to the pulsar times of arrival. For a $10^{-9}\,M_{\odot}$ companion to produce a timing amplitude of $\sim 1\,\mu{\rm s}$ , its orbital separation would need to be $\sim 4\times 10^{8}\,{\rm km}$ . This corresponds to an orbital period of $\sim 4\,{\rm yr}$ for an edge-on orbit around a $1.4\,M_{\odot}$ neutron star, and thus such systems are not interesting targets for the work discussed here, barring substantial orbital hardening.

A final astrophysical implication of the existence of primordial black hole-neutron star inspirals is that they would be natural targets for ground (and possibly space-based) gravitational-wave detectors. Figure 2 displays the characteristic strain predicted for binaries evolving solely through gravitational-wave emission, together with the sensitivity curves of current and future detectors. These estimates provide a reference for detectability; the effect of resonance locking on the SNR depends on the resulting frequency evolution and observing duration. However, Fig. 1 implies that typically, the SNR of a resonance locked system will be comparable to, or in the outspiral case, possibly much larger than, the corresponding point-particle system.

Very broadly, we find that $10^{-4}\,M_{\odot}$ primordial black holes will not be detectable by conventional standards at A+ sensitivity and a distance of $10\,\rm{Mpc}$ ( $\rm{SNR}\sim 5$ ), whereas $10^{-3}\,M_{\odot}$ primordial black hole-neutron star binaries should be detectable in principle ( $\mathrm{SNR}\sim 16$ at 10 Mpc). Sources with $M_{\rm BH}>10^{-6}\,M_{\odot}$ should be detectable in Cosmic Explorer, having $\mathrm{SNR}>10$ at $10\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ . Importantly, the signal-to-noise ratio of these systems scales comparatively weakly with mass ratio, $\mathrm{SNR}\propto\eta^{1/2}$ .

Nonlinear resonance locking has also been proposed in comparable-mass neutron-star binaries, where it may substantially affect the gravitational-wave phase while the binary continues to inspiral [17, 18]. In the intermediate mass ratio regime, both nonlinear modification and secular changes to neutron star rotation may be important. Assessing the implications for current ground-based searches for subsolar-mass black holes [47, 48, 49, 50] requires gravitational-wave models that include the locked evolution. Further derivations of the conditions for establishing and breaking a resonance lock, and of the effective tidal dissipation during the lock, are provided in the Supplemental Material [51, 15, 52, 53, 54].

Our results show that neutron star–primordial black hole binaries can exhibit orbital evolution strikingly different from that of typical compact binaries. Once a sustained resonance lock is established, dynamical tides can accelerate inspiral or drive outspiral despite continued gravitational-wave emission. In the latter case, the expanding orbit draws on the neutron star’s spin angular momentum, analogous to the outward migration of moons around rapidly rotating giant planets. These changes could leave distinctive signatures in pulsar timing and gravitational waves. Dynamical tides therefore merit particular attention in neutron-star binaries with large mass asymmetries, both when searching for these sources and when using them to constrain primordial black hole dark matter.

End Matter. Gravitational-wave emission during a close encounter provides one possible formation channel for neutron star–primordial black hole binaries [1, 55]. In the point-particle approximation, black holes with asymptotic relative speed $v_{\rm rel}$ become captured if their periastron distance is less than

$$ \displaystyle r_{p,\max}\simeq\left(\frac{85\pi}{6\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2/7}\frac{G\,\mu^{2/7}M_{\mathrm{NS}}^{5/7}}{c^{10/7}v_{\rm rel}^{4/7}}\,, \displaystyle\simeq 36.2\,{\rm km}\left(\frac{\mu}{10^{-3}M_{\odot}}\right)^{2/7}\!\!\left(\frac{M_{\mathrm{NS}}}{1.4M_{\odot}}\right)^{5/7}\!\!\left(\frac{v_{\rm rel}}{300\,{\rm km/s}}\right)^{-4/7}\!\!\!\!, $$

where $\mu=M_{\mathrm{BH}}M_{\mathrm{NS}}/(M_{\mathrm{BH}}+M_{\mathrm{NS}})\approx M_{\mathrm{BH}}$ is the reduced mass, and we use a fiducial relative speed of $300\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ for the numerical normalization [56]. The maximum periastron decreases with the primordial black hole mass and increases as the encounter speed decreases. For sufficiently small masses, capture outside the neutron star therefore requires slower encounters, which could be realized through many-body interactions. For passages near the stellar surface, dynamical tides may also contribute by transferring orbital energy into neutron star oscillation modes [56]. While estimates for these effects exist in the literature [10, 57, 58, 59], we believe a realistic encounter between a neutron star and primordial black hole should be governed essentially by nonlinear effects in the hydrodynamic flow of the neutron star. Multi-body encounters with other stars can also exchange orbital energy and angular momentum, modifying both capture and the subsequent evolution of the binary, and may be the dominant source of primordia capture [60]. A quantitative formation model must therefore assess these processes together with the primordial black hole abundance and encounter velocity distribution. In general, it is more challenging to capture a lower mass black hole onto a neutron star, either by tidal effects or gravitational-wave emission. However, at a fixed dark-matter mass fraction, lower mass black holes are more abundant, and therefore the odds of a capture of any primordial black hole onto a given neutron star are higher.

How is this scenario affected by the possibility of resonance locking? If the PBH becomes resonance locked, with $3I_{\mathrm{NS}}>I_{\mathrm{orb}}$ , which is generic for low-mass primordial black holes, then the system will instead outspiral toward the orbit where $3I_{\mathrm{NS}}=I_{\mathrm{orb}}$ . For a primordial black hole with $M_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{-8}\,M_{\odot}$ , this resonance-lock-breaking radius is $\gtrsim 5\times 10^{4}\,({GM_{\mathrm{NS}}}/{c^{2}})\simeq 10^{5}\,{\rm km}\sim 10^{-3}\,{\rm AU}$ , at which point gravitational inspiral times would exceed a Hubble time. Therefore, resonance locking may drive the primordial black hole far enough away from the neutron star to prevent coalescence. For higher mass primordial black holes ( $\sim 10^{-4}\,M_{\odot}$ ), the inspiral time from the resonance-lock breaking radius is only $\sim\rm{years}$ , and so these objects may very well merge with their host neutron stars eventually, but the predicted rate of such mergers is constrained to be very small.

If a $10^{-4}\,M_{\odot}$ primordial black hole did become resonance locked to a neutron star g-mode in a pulsar, close to the critical frequency, where $3I_{\mathrm{NS}}=I_{\mathrm{orb}}$ , then it would likely manifest as a sudden and apparently non-smooth transition to a much larger rate of period evolution. In particular, there would be a change in the braking index of the pulsar [61, 62]

$$ n\equiv\frac{\ddot{f}f}{\dot{f}^{2}}, $$

which during a lock (if other sources of braking are unimportant) becomes

$$ n=\frac{11I_{\mathrm{orb}}-21I_{\mathrm{NS}}}{3(I_{\mathrm{orb}}-3I_{\mathrm{NS}})}\frac{\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}}{\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}}. $$

Therefore, the braking index depends on the particular orbital configuration when the lock is achieved. If the configuration is such that $I_{\mathrm{orb}}\gg 3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , then the braking index will become $11/3\frac{\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}}{\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}}$ , which is less than $11/3$ by passivity. Nonetheless, the pulsar will be spinning up rather than spinning down, which is observed only in a handful of cases tied to acceleration of pulsars along the line-of-sight within globular clusters [63, 64]. It is also possible that a very small companion becomes resonance locked, in which case electromagnetic-driven spindown can become important, in addition to the tidal torque. This may serve to drive the companion to larger separations and lower frequencies, even if $I_{\mathrm{orb}}\gg 3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ . If $I_{\mathrm{orb}}<3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , on the other hand, and if $11I_{\mathrm{orb}}>21I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , then the pulsar will spin down but the braking index will be negative. Otherwise, if $I_{\mathrm{orb}}<3I_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , the pulsar will spin down with a positive braking index.

Finally, it may be the case that the process of resonance locking is not a clean monotonic transition in the detuning frequency, and even after the lock, the frequency executes cycles around the implied locking “fixed-point”. For example, in Ref. [16], a large number of possible locking phenomenologies are observed. In this case, the implied braking frequency of the pulsar could be transiently quite different from the one implied by Eq. (13). Complex behavior in the detuning frequency may occur on multiples of the damping timescale $1/\gamma$ , with $\omega/\gamma$ the mode quality factor. Since mode quality factors may be $\gtrsim 10^{8}$ for $1\,\mathrm{Hz}$ modes, the damping timescale may be $\sim\mathrm{years}$ for neutron stars. Therefore, extended observations of a large number of Galactic pulsars for long periods of time are likely the only way to detect such fluctuations.
