## I Supplemental Material

### I.1 Essential Physics

In the absence of tidal effects, the inspiral of two compact objects proceeds due to gravitational waves [1]

$$ \dot{E}\approx\dot{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}\overset{(\text{LO})}{=}-\frac{32c^{5}}{5G}\eta^{2}x^{5}f(e), $$

where $\eta={q}/{(1+q)^{2}}$ is the symmetric mass ratio, with $q=M_{\mathrm{BH}}/M_{\mathrm{NS}}$ the mass ratio (and the overset LO indicates the expression holds at leading order in the post-Newtonian expansion). Additionally, Kepler’s third law tells us that

$$ x\equiv\left(\frac{GM\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}}{c^{3}}\right)^{2/3}\overset{(\mathrm{LO})}{=}\frac{GM}{ac^{2}}, $$

with $\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}$ the orbital frequency of the binary, $M=M_{\mathrm{BH}}+M_{\mathrm{NS}}\approx M_{\mathrm{NS}}$ is the total mass of the binary. The function $f(e)$ depends only on the eccentricity and is an enhancement factor ( $f(e)\geq 1$ ) to the radiated power. There is no reason to expect that the longer-period binaries we look at here should have low eccentricity $e\sim 0$ , but unless otherwise stated we take $e=0$ because the tidal analysis is more complicated without this assumption. We do not expect the core conclusions to be changed by the inclusion of eccentricity, unless the eccentricity is excessively large.

The orbital energy of the system is

$$ E_{\mathrm{orb}}=-\frac{GM_{\mathrm{NS}}M_{\mathrm{BH}}}{2a}, $$

where $a$ is the semi-major axis (or the constant radius of the orbit, with our zero-eccentricity assumption). If the symmetric mass ratio is sufficiently small, then the inspiral timescale,

$$ \frac{t^{(\mathrm{GW})}_{\rm inspiral}}{GM/c^{3}}\sim\frac{E_{\mathrm{orb}}}{\dot{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}}=\frac{5c^{8}}{64G^{4}\eta}\frac{a^{4}}{M^{4}}, $$

is exceptionally long, even if $x$ is not small (equivalently, even if $a\sim\mathrm{tens\ of}\ M$ ).

Neutron stars have another important timescale, the dynamical timescale:

$$ t_{\rm dyn}\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{G\rho_{\rm c}}}\sim\sqrt{\frac{R_{\mathrm{NS}}c^{2}}{GM}}\frac{R_{\mathrm{NS}}}{c}. $$

Interestingly, the dynamical timescale of neutron stars is not too different from the gravitational timescale $t_{\rm grav}\equiv GM/c^{3}$ , since the compactness $C_{\mathrm{NS}}\equiv GM_{\mathrm{NS}}/(R_{\mathrm{NS}}c^{2})\approx 0.2$ for typical neutron stars.

Oscillation modes of a nonrotating, fluid star without stratification will be spaced fairly evenly in frequencies $\omega_{\rm{fund}}\gtrsim 2\pi/t_{\rm dyn}$ . Therefore, these modes are unlikely to be resonantly excited until $\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}\sim\omega_{\rm fund}$ , which requires $x=(2\pi)^{2/3}C_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , which, for a typical neutron stars means $x\sim 0.7$ , deep in the highly relativistic, dynamical regime. However, if the star is rotating, or if the star is stratified, or both, then there will be a spectrum of inertial modes, g-modes, or both. These modes have frequencies related to the rotation period or the Brunt-Väisälä frequency respectively, which in most cases, will be small compared to the fundamental frequency. This is what allows a neutron star mode to become resonantly locked.

In the inspiral of non-rotating neutron stars with comparable masses, orbital energy is transferred into (1) the physical deformations of the neutron star and (2) the gravitational field via tidal interactions. It is generally assumed that the most efficient energy transfer is mediated by the “slow” driving of the non-radial, fundamental $\ell=2$ mode of the star, which is called the equilibrium tide. In this case, the radiation-reaction timescale is very short owing to the relatively large symmetric mass ratio ( $\eta\sim 1/4$ ), so modes are not driven near their resonant frequencies for very long, as the frequency quickly chirps through the intrinsic oscillation frequency. Therefore, the system is dominated by the very large response of the equilibrium tide, and resonances are subdominant.

A consequence of this reasoning is the very strong scaling of the tidal response with the orbital separation. In particular, the amplitude of the equilibrium tidal mode (with frequency $\omega_{\ell mn}=\omega_{220}=\omega_{20}$ , since the star is nonrotating) is proportional to

$$ a_{20}(\omega)=\frac{1}{\omega^{2}_{20}-\omega^{2}}\frac{Q_{20}}{A_{20}^{2}}d_{20}(\omega) $$

where $Q_{20}$ is the tidal overlap, which is a purely geometric factor dependent on the mode profile, $A_{20}$ is a normalization factor, and $d_{20}\propto M_{\mathrm{BH}}/r^{3}$ is the tidal field induced by the black hole on the neutron star. The frequency $\omega$ is not close to $\omega_{20}\sim 2\pi/t_{\rm dyn}$ unless the orbit of the point particle has radius $r\sim R_{\mathrm{NS}}$ , so the mode amplitude is suppressed at low orbital frequency (large orbital separation) by both the tidal tensor and the dynamical response.

On the other hand, $g$ -modes and inertial modes will also have mode amplitudes

$$ a_{X}(\omega)=\frac{1}{\omega^{2}_{X}-\omega^{2}}\frac{Q_{X}}{A_{X}^{2}}d_{\ell}(\omega), $$

but may be resonantly excited at much lower frequencies, and thus, g-modes are not penalized as strongly by large orbital separation. In typical analyses of comparable-mass neutron star inspirals, the usual g-modes and inertial modes are neglected because of the small overlaps $Q_{X}$ between these modes and the tidal fields. However, fundamentally, the unimportance of these modes has more to do with the details of the driving mechanism. If the quality factor of the orbit is small, so that $\dot{a}/a$ is large, then, in frequency space, the driving force of the binary is delocalized.

To show this, let us consider a simplified model of the driving tidal force due to the companion

$$ d_{\ell}(\omega)\propto\int_{-T}^{T}d_{\ell}(t)\exp(-i\omega t)dt, $$

where $T$ is some timescale, which for our case we can imagine to be the time range where the orbit is close to resonance. The time dependent driving force of the neutron star tide due to the black hole will look like

$$ d_{2}(t)\propto\frac{M_{\mathrm{BH}}}{r^{3}(t)}e^{i\int\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}(t)dt}, $$

so $d_{2}(\omega)$ is given, in the stationary phase approximation, by

$$ d_{2}(\omega)\approx\frac{M_{\mathrm{BH}}}{r^{3}(t_{\omega})}\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt{\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}}(t_{\omega})}}\exp\left[i\Phi(t_{\omega})+i\frac{\pi}{4}\right], $$

assuming $\dot{\Omega}(t)>0$ and taking $\Phi(t)=\int_{-T}^{t}\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}(t)dt$ , with $t_{\omega}$ the stationary time at which $\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}(t_{\omega})=\omega$ . If $\dot{\Omega}$ is large, then the driving force is suppressed in the frequency domain. Conversely though, if $\dot{\Omega}$ is small, the force is amplified. This is the case for the post-Newtonian decay of binary orbits with small mass ratio. In particular, assuming no back reaction of the tide on the orbit, and no fluid dissipation, the maximum mode amplitude can be calculated according to [23],

$$ |a_{\alpha,\max}|\propto\frac{GM_{\mathrm{BH}}Q_{\alpha}}{a^{\ell_{\alpha}+1}}\left(\frac{\pi}{\dot{\Omega}_{\rm orb}}\right)^{1/2}_{\rm res}. $$

At some point in the orbit, fluid dissipation or nonlinear interactions can no longer be ignored. This will occur when the quality factor of the mode is comparable to $\Omega^{2}/\dot{\Omega}$ . For neutron star g-modes, the quality factor may be $\sim 10^{8}$ (though this is highly uncertain, as we discuss below). For generic values of mode frequencies and neutron star spins, these effects will become relevant around masses of $10^{-4}\text{--}10^{-3}\,M_{\odot}$ . However, it is important to recognize that $\omega_{X}=m(\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}-\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}})$ can have solutions with $\omega_{X}\sim 1\,\mathrm{Hz}$ , $\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}\sim 1\,\mathrm{Hz}$ , $\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}\ll\mathrm{1\,Hz}$ . In this case the inspiral is arbitrarily slow, and the resonance will almost certainly saturate. In this regime, further, the smallness of the black hole mass and the largeness of the orbital separation are less important than the detuning frequency. This is the regime of interest in this paper.

### I.2 Resonance Locking and Saturation

We first discuss the detailed physics by which resonance locking may occur, because similar concepts will be involved in describing the saturation of the resonance at $I_{\mathrm{orb}}/I_{\mathrm{NS}}\approx 3$ . We first describe the case of an object inspiraling from spatial infinity, because we view it as the most astrophysically relevant. In the absence of any substantial tidal effects, the system evolves under gravitational-wave damping alone:

$$ \displaystyle\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}} \displaystyle=\frac{-3\tau_{\mathrm{GW}}}{I_{\mathrm{orb}}}; \displaystyle\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{NS}} \displaystyle=0. $$

In practice, neutron stars are expected to have magnetic fields, and thus, they will spin down through magnetic braking as well. We discuss this briefly below.

If the resonance is sufficiently sharp, i.e. the mode width $\gamma_{\alpha}$ is narrow compared to the chirp rate, and if the mass ratio is small enough, then a lock will be achieved. Whether a lock can be established is ultimately determined by the efficiency of internal dissipation. This is quantified in the literature using a dimensionless number called the tidal quality factor [13]:

$$ Q_{\rm tide}\equiv 3k_{2}\frac{M_{\mathrm{BH}}}{M_{\mathrm{NS}}}\frac{R_{\mathrm{NS}}^{5}}{r^{5}}\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}t_{\mathrm{tide}}, $$

where $t_{\mathrm{tide}}$ is the time scale associated with tidal orbital energy being dissipated via tides, and $k_{2}$ is the static tidal Love number11 1 We use the static Love number to normalize the effective tidal quality factor. This choice does not neglect dynamical tides, whose effects enter through the physical tidal timescale $t_{\mathrm{tide}}$ . Changing the Love-number normalization rescales the quoted quality factor without changing the tidal torque, provided the response is treated consistently.. A large tidal quality factor corresponds to a long tidal evolution timescale. Near a mode resonance, however, dynamical tides can enhance the tidal torque and shorten $t_{\mathrm{tide}}$ , even when internal dissipation is weak. A necessary condition for resonance locking is that the available tidal torque can sustain the angular-momentum transfer required by Eq. (8). Establishing a lock also requires that the coupled evolution can reach and maintain this state.

Earlier calculations found insufficient tidal angular-momentum transfer to synchronize comparable-mass neutron-star binaries [25], and high-order g-modes have small overlaps with the companion’s tidal field [23, 20]. These results do not, however, exclude resonance locking in the extreme-mass-ratio systems considered here. A much lower-mass companion slows the gravitational-wave-driven evolution, allowing more time for a resonant response to develop, while weak mode damping can enhance the torque near resonance. We therefore compare next the attainable resonant tidal torque with the torque required to maintain a lock.

Let us then analyze this problem quantitatively, and consider the various channels that may allow a resonance lock to occur. To do this, we compare the tidal timescale $t_{\mathrm{tide}}$ to the inspiral timescale $t^{(\mathrm{GW})}_{\rm inspiral}$ from Eq. (S4). We first rewrite Eq. (S4) as

$$ \Omega_{\rm orb}t^{(\mathrm{GW})}_{\rm inspiral}=\frac{5}{64}\frac{1}{\eta}\left(\frac{c^{2}r}{GM}\right)^{5/2} $$

and Eq. (S14) as

$$ \Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}t_{\mathrm{tide}}=Q_{\rm tide}\times\frac{M_{\mathrm{NS}}r^{5}}{3k_{2}M_{\mathrm{BH}}R_{\mathrm{NS}}^{5}}. $$

We now need plausible estimates for the value of $Q_{\mathrm{tide}}$ . From [53], we rewrite the above expression in terms of the dimensionless dissipative tidal deformability $\Xi$ (using e.g. Eq. (24) of [53], for a circular orbit of only one extended object, taking $t_{\mathrm{tide}}=\left|E_{\mathrm{orb}}/\mathcal{F}_{\rm diss}\right|$ ),

$$ t_{\mathrm{tide}}=\frac{c^{13}r^{5}}{18G^{6}}\frac{1}{\Xi M_{\mathrm{BH}}M_{\mathrm{NS}}^{5}\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}^{2}}. $$

This gives

$$ \Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}t_{\mathrm{tide}}=\overbrace{\left[\frac{\Lambda}{16\Xi}\frac{c^{3}}{GM_{\mathrm{NS}}\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}}\right]}^{Q_{\mathrm{tide}}}\times\frac{r^{5}M_{\mathrm{NS}}}{3k_{2}M_{\mathrm{BH}}R^{5}_{\mathrm{NS}}}, $$

where

$$ \Lambda\equiv\frac{2}{3}k_{2}\left(\frac{c^{2}R_{\mathrm{NS}}}{GM_{\mathrm{NS}}}\right)^{5} $$

is the tidal deformability.

We have therefore developed an interpretation of the tidal quality factor as a measure of the conservative to dissipative tidal deformability, modulated by the dimensionless frequency. Constraints based on GW170817, and nuclear theory indicate that $\Lambda/\Xi$ is most likely at least 1, and potentially much greater than 1 [52]. This indicates that for the orbits we care about, the tidal quality factor from adiabatic tidal dissipation alone should be at least $\sim 10^{3}$ (though perhaps larger, e.g. $10^{6}-10^{9}$ ). From these estimates, we can then coarsely estimate

$$ \Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}t_{\mathrm{tide}}\sim 10^{3}\times\frac{1}{\eta}\times\frac{r^{5}}{R_{\mathrm{NS}}^{5}}\sim 10^{6}\times\left(\frac{2\,\rm{kHz}}{\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}}\right)^{10/3}, $$

which, for our problem, is $\sim 10^{16}$ . This tidal time scale is far too large to be important, which establishes that for such low frequency orbits, only dynamical tides can be relevant.

For dynamical tides, the above arguments are different because the tidal torque is dependent on the details of the mode being locked to. Following [19], we estimate the tidal torque as

$$ \tau_{\mathrm{tide}}=\frac{12\pi}{5}E_{\mathrm{orb}}\frac{M_{\mathrm{BH}}}{M_{\mathrm{NS}}}\left(\frac{R_{\mathrm{NS}}}{r}\right)^{5}Q_{\alpha}^{2}\left(\frac{\omega_{\alpha}\gamma_{\alpha}}{\delta\omega_{\alpha}^{2}+\gamma_{\alpha}^{2}}\right) $$

where $\omega_{\alpha}$ is the mode frequency, $\gamma_{\alpha}$ is the mode damping rate, $Q_{\alpha}$ is the tidal overlap of the mode, and we have taken $\ell=m=2$ for this estimate. We assume throughout this work that the mass ratio is sufficiently small and the internal sound speed is sufficiently large, so that excited resonant modes can be treated as standing waves [19].

Generally, tidal overlaps of high-order g-modes are expected to be small, which is primarily because these modes have many nodes and therefore are rapidly oscillating radially. For example, Ref. [54] gives $Q_{a}\sim 3.5\times 10^{-3}n_{a}^{-5/2}$ with $n_{a}$ the number of radial nodes. However, nonlinear combinations of modes may combine to form effective modes with much longer wavelengths, increasing the tidal overlap [26]. As it stands, computing the nonlinear oscillation spectrum of a neutron star at low frequency is a challenging task, in part because of the density of g-modes at low frequency and the incredibly small damping times of high-order g-modes. Furthermore, the equation of state of neutron stars is unknown, and even the relevant species which determine the compositional gradients (e.g. nucleons or hyperons) is unknown. We instead give the necessary condition for a resonance lock to occur, and leave to future work the task of determining which neutron star models are consistent with such conditions.

Evaluating Eq. (S21) for the torques induced through dynamical tides at exact resonance, $\delta\omega_{\alpha}=0$ , and using $M_{\mathrm{BH}}/M_{\mathrm{NS}}\simeq\eta\ll 1$ , gives the maximum tidal torque magnitude in the steady linear response:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|\tau_{\mathrm{tide}}|}{|E_{\mathrm{orb}}|}\sim 8\times 10^{-6}\frac{\eta}{10^{-3}}\left(\frac{10R_{\mathrm{NS}}}{r}\right)^{5}\frac{Q_{\alpha}^{2}}{(1\times 10^{-3})^{2}}\frac{\omega_{\alpha}/\gamma_{\alpha}}{10^{8}}. $$

Before comparing the available and required torques, let us discuss the damping assumed in the numerical normalization of Eq. (S22). We used here the illustrative value $\omega_{\alpha}/\gamma_{\alpha}=10^{8}$ , rather than a damping rate calculated for a specific neutron-star model. Electron shear viscosity contributes to the damping [65], with shorter-wavelength modes generally more strongly affected, while the rate depends on the mode eigenfunction, stellar temperature, superfluidity, and crustal physics [20]. Nonlinear mode interactions may introduce additional dissipation [27], depending on the driving amplitude and instability thresholds. A quantitative assessment of locking therefore requires the overlap and damping rate of the same mode in a specified stellar model. In general though, poorer internal dissipation should lead to larger torques when the mode is fully saturated.

Let us now compare the tidal torque to the gravitational-wave induced torque. For gravitational waves, the relevant torque is

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|\tau_{\mathrm{GW}}|}{|E_{\mathrm{orb}}|} \displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}}\frac{\dot{E}_{\mathrm{GW}}}{E_{\mathrm{orb}}}=\frac{1}{\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}t^{(\mathrm{GW})}_{\rm inspiral}} \displaystyle\sim 5\times 10^{-7}\frac{\eta}{10^{-3}}\left(\frac{x}{0.0175}\right)^{5/2}, $$

with $x$ again the post-Newtonian parameter defined in Eq. (S2). A necessary condition for resonance locking is that the maximum available tidal torque be at least as large as the torque required by Eq. (8), with the appropriate sign. Whether this condition is satisfied depends on the mode overlap and damping rate, together with the orbital and stellar moments of inertia. For low-order $g$ -modes, e.g. at $\sim 50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ , the mode overlap may be large enough that the necessary condition is possibly satisfied directly. For high-order g-modes, $\sim 1\,\mathrm{Hz}$ , nonlinearities would likely be necessary to generate sufficiently large tidal overlaps.

It’s also possible that additional torques act on the system which modify the dynamics. For example, electromagnetic spin-down torques may be important in normal pulsar systems. In this case, the torque balance as written in the main text would not be correct, although resonance locking may still be possible. In this case, though, magnetic field drag on the black hole should also be incorporated, which is nontrivial to compute. We leave this to future work.

The tidal torque expression Eq. (S22) assumes that saturation of the resonant instability is possible in the time before gravitational radiation drives the system out of resonance. This assumption hinges on a slow inspiral, and thus on a small symmetric mass ratio $\eta$ (equivalently, a small companion mass relative to the neutron star). Therefore, despite the fact that both torques scale with the symmetric mass ratio $\eta$ , the tidal torque implicitly scales much more strongly with $\eta$ because mode saturation will be possible only when $\dot{\Omega}_{\rm orb}/\Omega_{\rm orb}^{2}\ll\gamma_{\alpha}/\Omega_{\rm orb}$ . Strictly, to fully saturate the resonance within the pure linear model, $\dot{\Omega}_{\mathrm{orb}}\sim\gamma_{\alpha}^{2}$ . However, we assume the resonance saturates well before reaching the maximum amplitude through another, likely nonlinear, mechanism. It’s also possible that other processes amplify the mode amplitude transiently (such as a starquake), or slow down the inspiral transiently (such as a mean-motion resonance with another satellite), to allow locking. Nonetheless, the derivations we use here will not easily apply to near-equal mass binaries, unless the mode frequency is surprisingly fine-tuned to the NS spin frequency, so $\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}}$ at locking is $\ll 1\,\mathrm{Hz}$ . With a dense NS g-mode spectrum, though, this could nonetheless happen for some small number of equal mass binaries. If mode quality factors are lower, then saturation happens much faster, though the maximum torque the BH can provide in the locked phase is smaller as well.

Saturation of the resonant tidal energy transfer will occur before $I_{\mathrm{NS}}=I_{\rm orb}/3$ . There exist some general benchmarks for when the resonance-lock condition must break down. Nonlinearities very likely become important when the modes are driven to such large amplitudes; we give a discussion of one possible nonlinear effect in the next section.

### I.3 Dynamics of the system near resonance

When the resonance condition $\omega_{X}=m(\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}-\Omega_{\mathrm{orb}})$ is satisfied, the companion’s tidal field resonantly excites the neutron star’s $X$ -mode. In the absence of rotation, a mode of an isolated star with frequency $\omega_{X}$ is associated with a solution to the perturbed Einstein equations of the form

$$ \vec{\xi}(t,r,\theta,\phi)\propto\exp\left[i\left(\omega_{X}t-m\phi\right)\right]\vec{\xi}(r,\theta)\,, $$

where typically $\vec{\xi}$ is the Lagrangian displacement vector of the fluid. Using a model for resonant tidal excitation from Ho and Lai [15], and in the absence of external forces, the Newtonian equations of motion for the mode amplitude are

$$ \ddot{a}_{X}(t)-2iT_{X}\dot{a}_{X}+(\omega^{2}_{X}-2T_{X}\omega_{X})a_{X}=\\
\frac{M_{\mathrm{BH}}}{r^{3}}\left[\hat{Q}_{\ell m,\alpha}e^{i(-m\phi-\omega_{X}t)}-\hat{Q}_{\ell-m,\alpha}e^{i(m\phi-\omega_{X}t)}\right], $$

where $a_{X}$ is the complex mode amplitude and $\hat{Q}_{\ell m}$ represents22 2 This is $W_{\ell m}Q_{\ell m,\alpha}$ in the notation of [15]. We assume the neutron star spin is aligned with the orbit, which allows for several simplifications. the overlap of the mode with the tidal field. Finally $T_{X}$ represents the rotational contributions to the dynamics,

$$ T_{X}=-m\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}+i\int d^{3}x\rho\vec{\xi}_{X}\cdot\left(\vec{\Omega}_{\mathrm{NS}}\times\vec{\xi}_{X}\right). $$

In this work, we follow [13] and assume the inertial contributions to the equations of motion are negligible, $T_{X}=0$ . This is, in general, not a good assumption, but we expect our overall picture of resonance locking to remain unchanged by the introduction of inertial effects (though inertial modes may be an additional source of resonances, which may or may not lock efficiently [13]).

We do wish to model weak interactions with other system degrees of freedom, which can be taken to include inertial effects, damping, and nonlinearities (potentially including nonlinear interactions with other modes). We must therefore add to the right-hand side of Eq. (S26) an external force of the form

$$ f_{\rm ext}=f_{\rm ext}(t,a_{X},\dot{a}_{X},\dots). $$

Schematically then, Eq. (S26) becomes

$$ \ddot{a}_{X}+\omega_{X}^{2}a_{X}=A_{X}e^{im\Phi(t)}+f_{\rm ext}, $$

where $A_{X}(r)=M_{\rm BH}/r^{3}\hat{Q}_{\ell m,X}$ , $\Phi^{\prime}(t)=\phi^{\prime}(t)-\Omega_{\mathrm{NS}}(t)$ , and we have assumed the system is close to resonance, so $\omega_{X}=m\dot{\Phi}$ and the second term from Eq. (S26) is dominant. This simplified model captures the key details of the problem we are interested in.

We can analyze this system in the slowly varying envelope approximation, setting

$$ a_{X}=c_{X}e^{i\omega_{X}t} $$

to find

$$ 2i\omega_{X}\dot{c}_{X}=A_{X}e^{im\Phi(t)-i\omega_{X}t}+f_{\rm ext}e^{-i\omega_{X}t}. $$

For simplicity, we now consider a model for $f_{\rm ext}$ which will allow the problem to be analyzed

$$ f_{\rm ext}=-2\gamma\dot{a}_{X}-\beta a_{X}^{3}, $$

where $\gamma$ and $\beta$ should be small enough that these terms are unimportant when the amplitude of the system is small. The envelope equation then becomes

$$ 2i\omega_{X}\dot{c}_{X}=A_{X}e^{i\delta\phi(t)}-2i\gamma\omega_{X}c_{X}-\frac{3}{4}\beta|c_{X}|^{2}c_{X}. $$

Further decomposing $c_{X}=Re^{i\theta}$ , one finds

$$ \displaystyle\dot{R} \displaystyle=-\gamma R+\frac{A_{X}}{2\omega_{X}}\sin(\theta-\delta\phi); \displaystyle\dot{\theta} \displaystyle=\frac{3\beta}{8\omega_{X}}R^{2}+\frac{A_{X}}{2\omega_{X}R}\cos(\theta-\delta\phi), $$

so the nonlinear term modifies the resonance condition via a frequency shift

$$ \omega_{X}^{\prime}=\omega_{X}+\frac{3\beta}{8\omega_{X}}R^{2}. $$

The essential point of this analysis is that even if the resonance lock is maintained, nonlinear terms will eventually perturb the resonance condition slightly. In general, perturbations that push the system further into lock will lead to larger mode amplitudes and stronger nonlinear corrections. In this simple model, the mode resonance is pushed to higher frequency, so it is achieved at smaller orbital radius. There is a natural feedback mechanism in this system, where rapid dissipation from nonlinear terms will spin up the neutron star, while, on the other hand, slow dissipation will lead to larger mode amplitudes and stronger nonlinear corrections. The only effect that may change this qualitative picture is the emergence of a parametric instability. Still, we expect the emergence of such an instability to saturate and quickly lead to a large amount of internal dissipation in the star, which would also result in spin modifications. In general, nonlinear effects in the star will tend to lead to more possible relevant degrees of freedom which can couple to the tidal force, but also more possible mechanisms to dissipate stored mode energy.
